learn: The vowels are a, e, i, o and u. Every word has at least one vowel.
Short a says /a/ as in cat. Short e says /e/ as in bed. Short i says /i/ as in pig.
Short o says /o/ as in hot. Short u says /u/ as in sun.
lessons.try: Say each short vowel sound and think of one word for each.

learn: A blend is two consonants side by side. You can hear both sounds.
In "stop", you hear /s/ and /t/. In "frog", you hear /f/ and /r/.
Other start blends are bl, cl, gr, tr, sl and sp.
check: Which word starts with a blend?
lessons.try: Read these words: flag, crab, spin, slug, drum.

learn: Blends can come at the end of a word too.
"Hand" ends with nd. "Lamp" ends with mp. "Best" ends with st.
Say the word slowly so you can hear every sound.
check: How do you hear every sound in a word?
lessons.try: Read and write: tent, milk, jump, desk, list.

learn: Short a says /a/ as in cat. Many short words have it: map, bag, ham, sad, cap.
The pattern is consonant, vowel, consonant. We call it CVC.
In CVC words the vowel is usually short.
check: In CVC words the vowel is usually...
lessons.try: Read and write: map, bag, ham, sad, cap.

lessons.t: Short e and Short i Words
learn: Short e says /e/ as in bed: wet, pen, leg, ten.
Short i says /i/ as in pig: sit, win, lip, mix.
Listen carefully: pen and pin sound close but are different words.
lessons.try: Sort: pen, pin, bed, bid, ten, tin.

lessons.t: Short o and Short u Words
learn: Short o says /o/ as in hot: mop, dog, fox, log.
Short u says /u/ as in sun: cup, run, mud, bus.
Change o to u and hot becomes hut.
check: Change o in hot to u.
lessons.try: Write a list of five short o and five short u words.

learn: A blend is two consonants whose sounds we hear together: bl, cl, fl, gl, pl, sl.
Black, clap, flag, glad, plan, slip.
Say both sounds quickly: b-l, bl.
check: Which word starts with an l blend?
lessons.try: Read black, clap, flag, glad, plan and slip. Circle each blend.

learn: R blends: br, cr, dr, fr, gr, pr, tr.
Brick, crab, drum, frog, grin, press, trip.
The r sound comes right after the first sound.
check: Which word has an r blend?
lessons.try: Write five r-blend words and draw one.

learn: S blends: sk, sl, sm, sn, sp, st, sw.
Skip, slim, smell, snack, spot, stop, swim.
Hiss the s, then add the next sound.
lessons.try: Read skip, smell, snack and swim. Act out two.

learn: Blends can come at the end: -nd, -nt, -st, -mp, -sk, -lt.
Hand, tent, nest, jump, desk, belt.
Stretch the end of the word to hear both sounds.
lessons.try: Find the ending blend in hand, tent, nest, jump and desk.

learn: Some blends have three letters: str, spr, scr, spl.
Street, spring, scrub, splash.
Say all three sounds smoothly together.
lessons.try: Read street, spring, scrub, splash. Write each one.

learn: Read whole words with blends: clap, stomp, crust, blast.
Find the vowel first, then read the sounds around it.
Blend left to right without stopping.
check: Which word has a blend at the start and the end?
In The frog can swim, which word starts with fr?
lessons.try: Read: The frog can swim and jump in the pond.

learn: To spell a word with a blend, say it slowly and write every sound.
Do not drop a letter: flag needs both f and l.
Check by reading your word back.
lessons.try: Spell aloud and write: flag, drum, stop, nest, jump.

learn: Blends are everywhere: on signs, cereal boxes and in books.
A STOP sign has a blend. So does a PLAYGROUND sign.
Finding them helps you read faster.
check: Which word on a sign has a blend?
lessons.try: Hunt for ten words with blends in a book. Write them down.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Short Vowels and Blends
learn: You can read short vowel words and words with blends.
Blends come at the start, at the end and even in threes.
Say each sound and blend it smoothly.
check: Which word has a three-letter blend?
Which word ends with a blend?
What is the vowel in crab?
lessons.try: Read this sentence: The crab and the frog swam fast to the sand.

learn: A digraph is two letters that make one new sound.
s and h together say /sh/ as in ship and fish.
c and h together say /ch/ as in chin and lunch.
check: Two letters that make one sound
lessons.try: Find three things at home that have sh or ch in their names.

learn: t and h together say /th/ as in thumb and bath.
w and h together say /w/ as in when and whale.
Many question words start with wh: what, when, where, why and which.
check: Which is a wh question word?
What sound does th make in "thumb"?
lessons.try: Ask a family member three questions that start with wh.

learn: c and k together say /k/ at the end of short words like duck, sock and back.
n and g together say /ng/ as in sing, ring and king.
Digraphs help you read many more words.
check: What sound does ck make in "duck"?
lessons.try: Read: duck, rock, sing, long, sick, wing.

learn: A digraph is two letters that make one new sound.
Sh says /sh/ as in ship, shop, fish and wish.
Put your finger to your lips: shh!
check: A digraph is two letters that make...
In wish, sh is at the...
lessons.try: Read ship, shop, fish and wish. Where is sh in each?

learn: Ch says /ch/ as in chin, chop, lunch and rich.
It sounds like a sneeze: ah-choo!
Tch also says /ch/ after a short vowel: catch, match.
lessons.try: Read chin, chop, lunch, catch and match.

learn: Th has two sounds: soft in thin and thank, buzzy in this and that.
Put your tongue between your teeth to say th.
Bath, math and with end in th.
check: To say th, put your tongue between your...
Which word starts with buzzy th?
lessons.try: Read thin, thank, this, that, bath, math.

learn: Wh says /w/ in many words: when, what, where, which, why, whale.
Many question words start with wh.
Who is different: it says /h/.
check: Which question word starts with wh?
lessons.try: Ask a grown-up five questions that start with wh.

learn: Ck says /k/ at the end of a word after a short vowel.
Duck, sock, back, pick, truck.
If the vowel is short and the word ends in /k/, think ck.
lessons.try: Read duck, sock, back, pick and truck.

learn: Ng says /ng/ as in ring, sing, long and song.
The sound comes from the back of your nose.
Many words end in -ing: jumping, singing.
check: The ng sound comes from your...
lessons.try: Read ring, sing, long and song. Hum the ng sound.

learn: Some digraphs start words: ship, chip, thin, whip.
Changing the digraph changes the word.
Ship, chip and whip differ only at the start.
check: Change sh in ship to ch.
Change sh in ship to wh.
lessons.try: Change the start of ship to make chip and whip.

learn: Digraphs can end words: dish, much, path, back, sing.
Listen for the last sound to find the digraph.
Dish ends with /sh/. Path ends with /th/.
lessons.try: Find the ending digraph in dish, much, path, back, sing.

learn: Sort words by their digraph: sh, ch, th, wh, ck, ng.
Shell, cheese, thumb, wheel, clock, king.
Sorting helps your eyes and ears learn each pattern.
lessons.try: Sort twelve word cards into digraph groups.

learn: Read: The duck can swim in the pond. Chad has a red ship.
Find every digraph as you read.
Then read again more smoothly.
check: In The duck can swim, which word has a digraph?
In Chad has a red ship, which two words have digraphs?
Reading again helps us read more...
lessons.try: Read three sentences and underline the digraphs.

learn: When you hear /sh/, /ch/, /th/, /wh/, /k/ at the end, or /ng/, choose the digraph.
Fish needs sh. Lunch needs ch. Sing needs ng.
Check your spelling by reading it back.
lessons.try: Write a sentence with at least three digraph words.

learn: Digraphs are two letters that make one sound: sh, ch, th, wh, ck and ng.
They can come at the start or the end of words.
You can read and spell them!
check: Sh, ch and th are called...
lessons.try: Read: When will the chick and the duck sing?

lessons.t: Magic E Makes a Vowel Long
learn: When a word ends in e after one consonant, the e is silent.
The silent e makes the vowel before it say its name. This is a long vowel.
"Cap" becomes "cape". "Kit" becomes "kite".
check: Makes the vowel say its name
Can you hear the e at the end of "kite"?
lessons.try: Write "tap", then add an e. Read the new word.

learn: a with silent e: cake, game, lake.
i with silent e: bike, time, five.
o with silent e: home, rope, nose.
lessons.try: Read: rake, ride, bone, gate, pine, hole.

learn: u with silent e can say /yoo/ as in cube and mule, or /oo/ as in tube and flute.
e with silent e is less common: Pete, these.
When you see a word ending in e, try the long vowel first.
check: When a word ends in silent e, try...
lessons.try: Read: cute, rule, these, June.

learn: Silent e at the end of a word makes the vowel say its name.
Cap becomes cape. Tap becomes tape. Mad becomes made.
The pattern is a, consonant, e.
lessons.try: Add e to cap, tap, mad and can. Read the new words.

learn: Silent e makes i say its name: kit becomes kite, pin becomes pine.
Bike, time, ride and smile have long i.
The e is quiet, but it does a big job.
lessons.try: Add e to kit, pin, rid and dim. Read them.

learn: Silent e makes o say its name: hop becomes hope, not becomes note.
Home, rose, bone and stove have long o.
Read the word with and without e to hear the change.
lessons.try: Read hop and hope, not and note, rob and robe.

learn: Silent e makes u say its name: cub becomes cube, tub becomes tube.
Cute, mule and huge have long u. In rule and flute, u says /oo/.
Both are long u sounds.
lessons.try: Read cub and cube, tub and tube, cut and cute.

learn: Silent e can make e long in a few words: these, Pete, eve.
Long e is more often spelled ee or ea, which we will learn soon.
Silent e words with e are rare but real.
check: Which word has e with silent e?
Is e with silent e common?
lessons.try: Read these, Pete and theme.

learn: Without silent e, the vowel is usually short. With silent e, it is long.
Pan or pane? Kit or kite? Hop or hope?
Look at the end of the word to decide.
lessons.try: Read pairs: pan-pane, kit-kite, hop-hope, cut-cute.

learn: Silent e words make families: -ake: bake, cake, lake, make, take.
-ine: fine, line, mine, nine. -ope: hope, rope.
Know one, read them all.
check: Which word is in the -ake family?
Which word is in the -ine family?
Which word is in the -ope family?
lessons.try: Make a list of -ake and -ine words.

learn: When you hear a long vowel and one consonant at the end, think silent e.
Say the word. Write the vowel, the consonant, then e.
Make: m-a-k-e. Ride: r-i-d-e.
lessons.try: Spell aloud and write: make, ride, home, cute, game.

learn: Read: I like to ride my bike. The cake is on the plate.
Find each silent e word and its long vowel.
Read again with expression.
check: In Mike gave Jane a cute kite, how many silent e words?
In I like to ride my bike, which word has silent e?
What is on the plate? (The cake is on the plate.)
lessons.try: Read and underline silent e words: Mike gave Jane a cute kite.

learn: Read a short story: Jake and Kate went to the lake. They rode bikes. They ate cake.
Who went to the lake? What did they do?
Silent e words are now easy for you.
check: Where did Jake and Kate go?
lessons.try: Write your own three-sentence silent e story.

learn: Riddle: I am long and you can jump over me. What am I? A rope.
I am a number that comes after eight. Nine.
Riddles help you think about word meaning and spelling.
check: I am sweet and eaten at birthdays.
lessons.try: Make up a silent e riddle for a friend.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Silent E
learn: Silent e makes the vowel before it say its name.
It works for a, i, o, u and sometimes e.
Without it, the vowel is short.
check: Which word has a long vowel?
Silent e makes the vowel say its...
lessons.try: Read: Pete will hide the bone by the pine tree.

learn: Sometimes two vowels work together. We call them a vowel team.
ai says long a in the middle of words: rain, tail, paint.
ay says long a at the end: day, play, say.
check: What sound does ai make in "rain"?
At the end of a word
Which word has a vowel team?
lessons.try: Read: mail, train, stay, gray, wait.

learn: ee says long e: see, tree, feet.
ea often says long e too: eat, read, sea.
A rule to remember: when two vowels go walking, the first one often does the talking.
check: Which word has ea saying long e?
"When two vowels go walking," the first one...
lessons.try: Read: sheep, beach, green, leaf, meet.

learn: oa says long o: boat, coat, road.
ow can say long o: snow, grow, slow.
igh says long i: night, light, high.
lessons.try: Read: goat, show, bright, toad, flight.

learn: When two vowels go walking, the first one does the talking.
In ai, the a says its name: rain, train, mail, paint.
Ai usually comes in the middle of a word.
lessons.try: Read rain, train, mail and paint.

learn: Ay also says long a: day, play, say, tray.
Ay usually comes at the end of a word.
Ai in the middle, ay at the end.
lessons.try: Write five ay words.

learn: Ee says long e: see, tree, feet, green, sleep.
Two e letters side by side make it.
It can come in the middle or at the end.
lessons.try: Read see, tree, feet, green and sleep.

learn: Ea often says long e: eat, sea, read, leaf, team.
Sometimes ea says short e, as in bread and head.
Try long e first, then short e if it does not make sense.
lessons.try: Read eat, sea, leaf, team, bread and head.

learn: Oa says long o: boat, coat, road, soap, toad.
Oa usually comes in the middle of a word.
The o does the talking; the a is quiet.
check: In oa, which letter is quiet?
lessons.try: Read boat, coat, road and soap.

learn: Ow can say long o: snow, grow, show, bowl.
Ow can also say /ow/ as in cow and how. We will learn that later.
Try both sounds and pick the one that makes a word.
check: Which word has long o spelled ow?
If one sound does not make a word...
lessons.try: Read snow, grow, show and bowl.

learn: Igh says long i: high, light, night, right, bright.
The g and h are both silent.
Three letters make one sound.
check: In igh, which letters are silent?
lessons.try: Read high, light, night, right and bright.

lessons.t: ie and y Say Long i
learn: Ie can say long i: pie, tie, lie.
Y at the end of short words says long i: my, by, fly, cry.
Y at the end of longer words says long e: happy, baby.
lessons.try: Read pie, tie, my, fly, happy and baby.

learn: Oo can say /oo/ as in moon, food, zoo.
Oo can also say /oo/ as in book, look, foot.
Read the word both ways if you need to.
check: Moon has the same oo sound as...
Book has the same oo sound as...
lessons.try: Sort: moon, book, food, look, zoo, foot.

learn: Long a can be a_e, ai or ay. Long e can be ee or ea. Long o can be o_e, oa or ow.
Use what you know: ay at the end, ai in the middle.
When unsure, write it two ways and see which looks right.
lessons.try: Spell: play, rain, feet, boat, snow.

learn: Read: The goat ate the green leaves by the road.
Find the vowel teams: oa, ee, ea, oa.
Vowel teams make reading longer words possible.
check: In The goat ate the green leaves, which word has oa?
lessons.try: Read a short book and list five vowel team words.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Vowel Teams
learn: Vowel teams are two or three letters that make one vowel sound.
Ai, ay, ee, ea, oa, ow, igh, ie and oo are teams you know.
When two vowels go walking, the first one often does the talking.
lessons.try: Read: The night train is bright and fast as it goes by the sea.

learn: Some words appear so often that we learn them by sight.
Words like the, said, was, have, they and could do not always follow the rules.
Knowing them quickly helps you read smoothly.
check: Do sight words always follow the rules?
lessons.try: Practise reading these until they are fast: the, said, was, they, have, what.

learn: Good readers make their voice match the story.
A question mark means your voice goes up. An exclamation mark means read with feeling.
A period means stop for a short breath.
check: What does a question mark tell your voice?
What does an exclamation mark mean?
lessons.try: Read "Oh no!" and "Is it you?" with the right voice.

learn: If a sentence does not make sense, go back and read it again.
Ask: Does that look right? Does that sound right? Does that make sense?
Rereading helps you fix mistakes and understand more.
check: What do you do if a sentence does not make sense?
lessons.try: Read a page of a book twice. Notice how the second time is smoother.

learn: Fluency means reading smoothly, at a good speed, with feeling.
Fluent readers sound like they are talking.
Fluency helps you understand what you read.
check: Fluent readers sound like they are...
lessons.try: Listen to a grown-up read a page smoothly. Then read it yourself.

learn: Read groups of words together: the big dog / ran up / the hill.
Phrases make reading sound natural.
Do not stop after every word.
check: Should we stop after every word?
lessons.try: Read a sentence in phrases. Draw a slash between each phrase.

learn: Punctuation tells us how to read.
Stop at a period. Raise your voice at a question mark. Sound excited at an exclamation mark.
Pause a little at a comma.
check: At a question mark our voice goes...
lessons.try: Read: Stop. Who is it? It is a bear!

learn: Show how characters feel with your voice.
A scared mouse squeaks. A big giant booms.
Expression makes stories come alive.
lessons.try: Read a line in a happy voice, a sad voice and a scared voice.

lessons.t: Speed: Not Too Fast, Not Too Slow
learn: Read at a just-right speed, like talking.
Too fast and you make mistakes. Too slow and it is hard to understand.
Practice makes your speed grow.
check: As fast as a race car
lessons.try: Time yourself reading a page. Read it again tomorrow. Did you get faster?

learn: In echo reading, a grown-up reads a line and you read it back like an echo.
You copy their speed and expression.
Echo reading helps you sound fluent.
check: In echo reading, you read the line...
lessons.try: Echo read a poem with a grown-up.

learn: Partner reading means taking turns reading pages with a buddy.
The listener follows along and helps if needed.
Say: Try that again or Good job!
lessons.try: Partner read a book, switching each page.

learn: Readers' theater is reading a story like a play, each person reading a part.
No costumes needed. Your voice does the acting.
Practice your part so you can read it smoothly.
check: In readers' theater, each person reads a...
In readers' theater, what does the acting?
lessons.try: Read a short play with your family, each person taking a part.

learn: Poems have rhythm and rhyme, which help us read smoothly.
Read a poem many times until it flows.
Clap the beat as you read.
check: Reading a poem many times makes it...
While reading a poem you can clap the...
lessons.try: Read a short poem three times. Clap the beat.

learn: Good readers notice when something does not make sense.
They stop, look at the word again and fix it.
Ask: Does that sound right? Does it look right?
check: When something does not make sense, good readers...
Fixing your own mistake is called...
lessons.try: While reading, fix one mistake by yourself.

learn: Reading at home for 20 minutes each day makes you a stronger reader.
Read to someone, with someone or by yourself.
Keep a reading log of what you read.
check: How long should you try to read each day?
lessons.try: Start a reading log. Write the title and minutes each day.

learn: Fluent readers read smoothly, at a good speed, with expression.
They read in phrases, use punctuation and fix mistakes.
Practice makes fluent readers.
lessons.try: Read your favorite page to a grown-up with your best expression.

learn: A noun is a word for a person, place or thing.
Teacher, park and ball are nouns.
Names of special people and places, like Maya or Texas, start with a capital letter.
check: Which noun needs a capital letter?
lessons.try: Find five nouns in your room.

learn: Add s to most nouns to show more than one: cat, cats.
Add es to words that end in s, x, ch or sh: box, boxes; dish, dishes.
Some words change: one child, two children.
lessons.try: Write the "more than one" word for: dog, fox, bus, cup.

learn: A verb is an action word. It tells what someone does.
Jump, eat, read and swim are verbs.
Add ed to show it already happened: jump, jumped.
lessons.try: Act out three verbs and have someone guess them.

learn: A noun names a person, place, animal or thing.
People nouns: teacher, mom, baby, doctor, friend.
Ask: Is it a person? Then it is a people noun.
check: Which word is a people noun?
A noun names a person, place, animal or...
lessons.try: List five people nouns from your family or school.

learn: Place nouns name where things are: school, park, kitchen, beach, city.
You can go to a place noun.
Ask: Can I go there?
lessons.try: Draw three places you like and label them.

learn: Animal nouns: dog, frog, eagle, whale. Thing nouns: cup, ball, chair, book.
You can see and touch most thing nouns.
All of these are nouns.
lessons.try: Sort ten nouns into animals and things.

learn: A proper noun names a special person, place or thing: Maria, Arizona, Monday.
Proper nouns begin with a capital letter.
Dog is a common noun. Rover is a proper noun.
check: A proper noun starts with a...
lessons.try: Write your name, your town and the day of the week with capitals.

lessons.t: Adding s for More Than One
learn: Most nouns add s to mean more than one: cat to cats, book to books.
One is singular. More than one is plural.
Look for the s at the end.
lessons.try: Make these plural: hat, dog, bird, car.

learn: Nouns ending in s, x, ch or sh add es: bus to buses, box to boxes, lunch to lunches, dish to dishes.
Es adds a new syllable: box-es.
Clap to hear it.
lessons.try: Make plural: fox, wish, glass, bench.

learn: A verb shows action: run, jump, eat, read, swim.
Ask: Can I do it? Then it is an action verb.
Every sentence needs a verb.
lessons.try: Act out five verbs for someone to guess.

learn: Verbs can tell about now or the past.
Now: I jump. Before: I jumped. Many past verbs add -ed.
Yesterday words need past verbs.
lessons.try: Change to the past: play, walk, help, kick.

learn: Add -ing to show something is happening right now: is running, are reading.
Is and are go with -ing verbs.
Some words double the last letter: run to running, sit to sitting.
lessons.try: Write: I am ___ing. Fill in five verbs.

learn: One noun takes a verb with s: The dog runs. More nouns do not: The dogs run.
Say it aloud to check that it sounds right.
This is called agreement.
check: Nouns and verbs that match show...
lessons.try: Fix: The cats sleeps. The bird sing.

learn: Adjectives tell about nouns: big, red, soft, happy, three.
They answer: What kind? How many? Which color?
A big red ball has two adjectives.
check: In a big red ball, the adjectives are...
lessons.try: Describe your favorite toy with three adjectives.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Nouns and Verbs
learn: Nouns name people, places, animals and things. Proper nouns get capitals.
Verbs show action and can tell now or past.
Adjectives describe nouns.
check: In The happy dog ran, the verb is...
In The happy dog ran, the adjective is...
lessons.try: Write a sentence and label the noun, the verb and an adjective.

learn: A sentence is a complete thought.
It tells who or what, and what they do: The dog runs.
It starts with a capital letter and ends with a mark.
lessons.try: Write a sentence about your favourite food.

learn: A telling sentence ends with a period.
An asking sentence ends with a question mark.
A sentence with strong feeling ends with an exclamation mark.
lessons.try: Write one telling, one asking and one excited sentence.

learn: Adjectives describe nouns: the big, brown dog.
Details make writing more interesting to read.
We can join two ideas with and, but or because: I was tired, so I went to bed.
check: The fluffy cat slept in the sun.
lessons.try: Make "The cat sat." more interesting by adding two describing words.

learn: A sentence tells who or what, and what they do.
The cat (who) naps in the sun (what it does).
Without both parts, it is not a complete sentence.
check: In The dog barks, who is it about?
lessons.try: Finish: The bird ___. My friend ___.

learn: Use a capital letter at the start of every sentence.
Also for names, the word I, days and months.
Capitals tell readers something important.
lessons.try: Fix the capitals: on monday i saw sam.

lessons.t: Periods, Question Marks and Exclamation Marks
learn: A telling sentence ends with a period.
An asking sentence ends with a question mark.
A strong feeling ends with an exclamation mark.
check: Where is my hat ends with...
A telling sentence ends with a...
lessons.try: Write one of each kind of sentence.

learn: Questions often start with who, what, where, when, why or how.
They end with a question mark.
Questions help us learn more.
check: Which word often starts a question?
lessons.try: Write three questions to ask a grandparent.

learn: Use commas between three or more things in a list.
I like apples, grapes and pears.
Commas help the reader pause.
check: I see a cat, a dog and a bird.
I see, a cat a dog and a bird.
I see a cat a dog and, a bird.
Commas go between things in a...
lessons.try: Write a list sentence about your favorite foods.

learn: Details make sentences interesting.
I saw a dog. becomes I saw a fluffy brown dog at the park.
Add who, what, where, when or how.
check: The tall boy ran to the pool.
lessons.try: Add details to: The boy ran.

learn: We can join two short sentences with and.
I like cats. I like dogs. becomes I like cats and dogs.
Joining makes writing smoother.
check: Join: I have a pen. I have a pad.
I have a pen and a pad.
lessons.try: Join: Sam ran. Sam jumped.

learn: Because tells why.
I am happy because it is my birthday.
Use because to give reasons.
check: I wore a coat because it was cold.
lessons.try: Finish: I like school because ___.

learn: Order words show when things happen: first, next, then, after that, finally.
First I woke up. Next I ate breakfast. Finally I went to school.
They help readers follow along.
check: Which word comes at the end?
lessons.try: Write how to make a sandwich using order words.

learn: Strong verbs paint a picture. Instead of went, try raced, crept, skipped.
The mouse crept is better than the mouse went.
Choose verbs that show exactly what happened.
check: Which is a stronger verb than went?
The mouse ___ quietly past the cat.
lessons.try: Change went to a stronger verb in three sentences.

learn: Use a checklist: Capital? Spaces? Ending mark? Does it make sense?
Read your sentence out loud to check.
Fix one thing at a time.
check: What should a sentence start with?
lessons.try: Check three of your sentences with the checklist.

learn: Good sentences have a subject and action, capitals and ending marks.
Details, strong verbs, and, because and order words make them better.
Check your writing every time.
check: The frog jumped into the pond.
lessons.try: Write five good sentences about your weekend.

learn: Characters are the people or animals in a story.
The setting is where and when the story happens.
Authors give clues about characters through what they say and do.
check: The people or animals in a story
Where and when the story happens
How do we learn about characters?
lessons.try: Name the characters and setting of a story you read this week.

learn: Stories have a beginning, a middle and an end.
Often there is a problem in the middle that the characters must solve.
In "The Little Red Hen", the hen asks for help, nobody helps, so she does the work herself and eats the bread.
check: Where is the problem often found?
In "The Little Red Hen", who makes the bread?
Which words help retell a story?
lessons.try: Retell a story you know using first, next, then and last.

learn: Many stories teach a lesson, called a moral.
Aesop's fable "The Tortoise and the Hare" teaches that slow and steady wins the race.
Think about what a character learned by the end.
check: Who wins in "The Tortoise and the Hare"?
The lesson of that fable is...
Slow and steady wins the race
lessons.try: Tell someone the lesson of a story you like.

learn: The main character is who the story is mostly about.
Other characters help or cause trouble.
In The Little Red Hen, the hen is the main character.
check: The main character is who the story is...
In The Little Red Hen, the main character is the...
lessons.try: Name the main character and two other characters in a story you know.

learn: We describe characters by how they look, act and feel.
The Little Red Hen is hard-working. The other animals are lazy.
Use clues from the words and pictures.
check: We describe characters by how they...
Clues come from the words and...
lessons.try: Describe a character with three words.

learn: The setting tells where and when.
Authors give clues: a dark forest at night, a sunny beach in summer.
The setting can change during the story.
check: A sunny beach in summer is a...
Can a setting change in a story?
lessons.try: Draw the setting of a story with three details.

learn: Most stories have a problem and a solution.
The problem is what goes wrong. The solution fixes it.
In The Lion and the Mouse, the lion is trapped; the mouse chews the net.
check: In The Lion and the Mouse, the problem is...
lessons.try: Tell the problem and solution in a story you know.

learn: Retell a story with beginning, middle and end.
Use order words: first, next, then, last.
Include the important parts only.
lessons.try: Retell The Three Billy Goats Gruff in four sentences.

learn: Characters' feelings can change during a story.
A character may start sad and end happy.
Ask: Why did the feeling change?
check: A character might start sad and end...
lessons.try: Draw a character at the start and end. Show their feelings.

learn: Compare two characters: how are they alike and different?
The tortoise is slow and steady. The hare is fast but proud.
A Venn diagram can show the comparison.
check: A Venn diagram shows how things are...
lessons.try: Make a Venn diagram of the tortoise and the hare.

learn: A fable is a short story that teaches a lesson.
Fables often have talking animals.
Aesop told many fables long ago.
lessons.try: Read a fable and tell its lesson.

learn: Folktales are old stories passed down by telling.
Every culture has folktales. Anansi the spider comes from West Africa.
Folktales often have tricksters and magic.
lessons.try: Ask a family member to tell you an old story.

learn: Poems use few words, rhythm and often rhyme.
They can be funny, sad or full of wonder.
Poems are made of lines, and sometimes stanzas.
check: A group of lines in a poem is a...
lessons.try: Read a poem aloud. Find two rhyming words.

learn: Sometimes a character tells the story using I. Sometimes a narrator tells it.
I went to the park means a character is telling.
She went to the park means a narrator is telling.
check: If the story uses I, who tells it?
She went to the park is told by a...
The person telling a story is the...
lessons.try: Find a book where a character tells the story.

learn: Stories have characters, setting, problem and solution.
Fables teach lessons. Folktales are passed down.
Good readers retell, compare and find the lesson.
check: A short story with a lesson is a...
The tortoise and the hare are...
The person telling the story is the...
lessons.try: Retell a fable and tell its lesson.

learn: Fiction stories are made up. Nonfiction tells true facts.
A book about real sharks is nonfiction. A story about a talking shark is fiction.
We read nonfiction to learn.
check: A story about a talking shark is...
lessons.try: Find one fiction and one nonfiction book.

learn: Nonfiction books have helpers called text features.
A title tells the topic. Headings tell what each part is about. Captions explain pictures.
A table of contents tells which page each part is on.
check: What tells which page a part is on?
lessons.try: Find a heading and a caption in a nonfiction book.

learn: The main topic is what the whole text is about.
Key details are facts that tell more about the main topic.
In a text about frogs, a key detail might be "Frogs start life as tadpoles."
check: What the whole text is about
Which is a key detail about frogs?
lessons.try: Read a short nonfiction page. Say the main topic and two details.

learn: Headings are titles for parts of a nonfiction book.
They tell what each part is about.
Use headings to find what you need.
check: Headings tell what each ___ is about.
lessons.try: Find three headings in a nonfiction book.

learn: Bold words are darker. They are important words.
A glossary at the back tells what the bold words mean.
It is like a small dictionary for the book.
lessons.try: Find a bold word and look it up in the glossary.

learn: A diagram is a picture with labels that shows parts or how something works.
A diagram of a plant labels roots, stem and leaves.
Diagrams help us see information.
check: A diagram is a picture with...
lessons.try: Draw a diagram of a bicycle with four labels.

learn: The main topic is what the whole text is mostly about.
Look at the title and the headings for clues.
A book called Sharks is about sharks.
check: The main topic is what the text is...
Clues to the topic come from the...
A book called Sharks is about...
lessons.try: Tell the main topic of a nonfiction book you read.

learn: Key details tell more about the main topic.
If the topic is frogs, a key detail is: frogs lay eggs in water.
Details answer who, what, where, when, why and how.
check: Key details tell more about the...
Which is a key detail about frogs?
lessons.try: Write two key details about a topic.

learn: Before reading, ask what you wonder. While reading, look for answers.
After reading, answer: What did I learn?
Questions keep your brain busy.
check: After reading, ask: What did I...
lessons.try: Write two questions before reading about whales. Find the answers.

learn: Photos show real things. Captions tell about the photos.
Read the caption to learn more facts.
A caption might say: A baby sea turtle heads to the ocean.
check: Where do baby sea turtles head?
lessons.try: Find a photo and caption in a magazine or book.

learn: The table of contents at the front lists the chapters.
The index at the back lists topics with page numbers in ABC order.
Use them to find information fast.
lessons.try: Use an index to find a topic.

learn: Two books on the same topic may give different details.
Read both and tell what is the same and different.
Using more than one book helps us learn more.
check: Two books on one topic may give...
We compare by finding what is...
lessons.try: Read two books about the same animal. Compare them.

learn: A fact can be proven. An opinion is what someone thinks or feels.
Fact: Dogs have four legs. Opinion: Dogs are the best pets.
Words like best and favorite often show opinions.
lessons.try: Write one fact and one opinion about dogs.

learn: Nonfiction can include charts and lists.
A chart organizes facts in rows and columns.
Read the title first, then the rows.
lessons.try: Make a chart of three animals and what they eat.

learn: Nonfiction uses headings, bold words, glossaries, diagrams, captions and indexes.
Find the main topic and key details.
Know the difference between a fact and an opinion.
check: The main topic is what the text is...
Dogs are the best pets is a...
lessons.try: Make a fact sheet about an animal with a heading, a diagram and a caption.

learn: An opinion is what you think or feel.
When you write an opinion, say what you think and give a reason.
"I think cats are the best pets because they are soft and quiet."
check: What should go with an opinion?
lessons.try: Write your opinion about your favourite season and one reason.

learn: Informative writing teaches facts about a topic.
Name the topic, give some facts, then write an ending.
"Bees are insects. They make honey. They help flowers grow. Bees are helpful."
check: Which is a fact about bees?
lessons.try: Write three facts about an animal you know.

learn: A narrative tells about something that happened, in order.
Use words like first, then and at the end.
Tell how you felt. Then share your writing with a friend and listen to their ideas.
lessons.try: Write about something fun you did, in three parts.

learn: Opinion writing tells what you think.
Start with a clear sentence: I think dogs are the best pets.
Use words like I think, I believe, my favorite.
check: I think summer is the best season.
lessons.try: Write an opinion sentence about your favorite season.

learn: Give reasons with because.
Dogs are the best because they are loyal and fun.
Two or three reasons make your opinion strong.
check: How many reasons make an opinion strong?
lessons.try: Write two reasons for your opinion.

learn: End your opinion writing by saying your opinion again.
That is why dogs are the best pets!
A good ending wraps up your ideas.
check: That is why dogs are the best! is an...
lessons.try: Finish your opinion piece with an ending sentence.

learn: Informative writing teaches facts.
Start by naming the topic: Bees are amazing insects.
Choose a topic you know about.
lessons.try: Write a topic sentence about an animal.

learn: Add facts about your topic: Bees make honey. Bees help flowers grow.
Use books to find facts.
Write each fact in its own sentence.
check: Which is a fact about bees?
Each fact goes in its own...
lessons.try: Write three facts about your topic.

learn: End with a closing sentence: Bees are important to our world.
The closing sums up the topic.
Add a picture with labels.
check: Bees are important to our world.
lessons.try: Finish your informative writing with a closing and a labeled picture.

learn: A narrative tells a story of something that happened.
Tell events in order with first, next, then, last.
Include feelings: I felt so excited!
check: I felt so excited shows a...
lessons.try: Write about a fun day in four sentences.

learn: Add details: what you saw, heard and did.
End with how it turned out or how you felt.
A good ending makes the reader feel finished.
check: Details tell what you saw and...
A good ending makes the reader feel...
An ending can tell how you...
lessons.try: Add two details and an ending to your narrative.

learn: Revising means changing your writing to make it better.
Add details, choose stronger words or move sentences.
Read it to a partner and listen to their ideas.
lessons.try: Revise one piece by adding two details.

learn: Editing means fixing capitals, punctuation and spelling.
Use a checklist and read slowly.
Edit after revising.
lessons.try: Edit your writing using a checklist.

learn: Publishing means making a final copy to share.
Write neatly, add pictures and a title.
Share your writing with your class or family.
lessons.try: Publish one piece and read it aloud to someone.

learn: You can write opinions, information and stories.
You plan, write, revise, edit and publish.
Writers share ideas with the world.
check: A story about what happened is a...
lessons.try: Write and publish a piece of your choice.
